content.title: About
content.content: Mung beans (Vigna radiata) are small green legumes widely used in Asian cuisine. When cooked they become tender, mildly sweet, and retain their nutritional value. They are commonly added to soups, salads, porridges, and used as a filling for spring rolls.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mung beans are one of the oldest cultivated legumes, with cultivation dating back over 5,000 years in India and China.
The seeds can sprout in 1–2 days, producing nutrient‑dense microgreens.
In China, mung beans are often used to make a sweet dessert soup called "sweet mung bean soup."
The beans fix nitrogen in the soil, improving its fertility.
In Japan, boiled mung beans are served as a salted snack called "edamame."

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked mung beans provides about 14 g of protein, making them an excellent protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Mung beans raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for diabetes management and weight control.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain gut health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B6, and folate contribute to energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals and antioxidants
items.content: Mung beans provide iron, magnesium, potassium, and antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes, including mung beans.

items.title: Phytates
items.content: Phytate content can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and cooking help mitigate this.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause bloating in sensitive people; gradual introduction to the diet reduces the effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked mung beans can be added to soups, salads, rice dishes, used as a filling for spring rolls, or blended into a dip. They also work well in vegetarian patties or as a base for sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked mung beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portioned bags for up to 3 months. Discard any beans with an off‑smell or signs of spoilage.
